title: Owen-Stoltenberg: Accept or Resist?
sources: UN S/26486 (23 September 1993) — ICFY transmission of the Invincible package
UN S/26922 (21 December 1993) — ICFY Steering Committee report on the Assembly rejection
content:
On 20 September 1993, aboard HMS Invincible, David Owen and Thorvald Stoltenberg presented their Union of Three Republics plan — a confederal partition of Bosnia into three ethnically defined republics. The Sarajevo Presidency accepted narrowly, conditional on territorial concessions in eastern Bosnia: the return of Drina-valley enclaves and access to the Posavina corridor.

The conditional acceptance threw the decision to the Bosnian Assembly, which convened on 29 September 1993. The ICFY record (UN S/26486 and S/26922) documents the procedural sequence: a Presidency that accepted under pressure at Geneva, and an Assembly that rejected the partition formula outright when the territorial conditions went unmet. The plan died on that vote.

The choice the Assembly faced was sharp. Ratifying the Presidency's conditional acceptance would have signed Bosnia onto a three-republic confederation — institutionalizing the ethnic partition the government had resisted since 1992 — in exchange for territorial adjustments that the warring parties had no incentive to honour. Rejecting it preserved the unitary claim at the cost of foreclosing the most concrete settlement then on offer and prolonging the war.

The Invincible package was also the last of the great-power partition plans to bear David Owen's name. Its failure closed the European-led mediation phase of the war and opened the way for the more coercive American diplomacy of the Contact Group and, ultimately, Dayton. The Assembly's vote therefore carried weight beyond the plan itself: it signalled whether Sarajevo would settle the war on the partition terms then available, or hold out for terms that only sustained military and diplomatic pressure could later extract.

The posture recorded here is the procedural hinge between a 1993 confederal settlement and the two-more-years of war that history delivered before Dayton.
